title: Mary's falling asleep (15 August)
hook: Orthodox keep the Dormition, Catholics the Assumption; many Protestants simply honor Mary as a faithful disciple

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Transfiguration, a mountain of light on a date that also holds a darker one. Your line was two lights. Where did a light remind you to pray or hope for peace? Day one thousand forty-eight.

Here is an Orthodox icon. A woman lies on a bier, eyes closed, hands folded. The apostles crowd around her, some bending close, some weeping. Behind the bier stands Jesus, in light. And in his arms he holds a tiny figure wrapped in white, like a newborn. It's her soul. At the start of the Gospels, she carried him as a baby. In this picture, he carries her. The woman is Mary, the mother of Jesus. Orthodox Christians call this moment her falling asleep. Today's word: Dormition.
screen: `AN ICON: A WOMAN ON A BIER.`
`JESUS HOLDS HER SOUL LIKE A CHILD.`
`SHE CARRIED HIM. NOW HE CARRIES HER.`

segments.voice: Scripture follows Mary to a last scene, and then goes quiet. In Luke, her answer to the angel ends in a yes: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." At the cross, in John's Gospel, Jesus gives her into a disciple's care: "Behold thy mother! And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home." The last time Acts names her, she is praying with the apostles: "Mary the mother of Jesus." After that, silence. The New Testament never tells how her life ended. So the churches have three ways of keeping this day, and it's fair to name each one plainly. Orthodox Christians keep the Dormition. Dormition means falling asleep. The New Testament can speak of the faithful dead as sleeping; of Stephen, stoned to death in Acts, the King James says simply, "he fell asleep." The Orthodox tradition holds that Mary truly died, surrounded by the apostles, and that her Son received her soul, as the icon shows, and that her body too was then taken up to heaven. Catholics keep the fifteenth of August as the Assumption. Catholic teaching holds that at the end of her earthly life, Mary was taken up, body and soul, into the glory of heaven. Protestants who don't hold either as a teaching give a plain reason: scripture doesn't tell the story. They honor her as Luke does, as the faithful disciple who said yes and kept saying it, all the way to the cross and the upper room. Some keep the day as a plain festival of Mary. Three churches, three ways. What they share is the woman in Luke who said, "all generations shall call me blessed," and a sense that the one who carried Jesus was not forgotten by him.

Here's the practice: honor a faithful mother. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a woman who carried someone: a mother, a grandmother, a foster mother, an aunt, a neighbor who raised half the street. She may be living or she may have died. Think of one specific thing she did, again and again, without applause. A packed lunch. A light left on. If you pray, you can thank God for her by name. If you don't, just hold her in mind with thanks. If she has died, you might picture her, the way the icon does, being carried now. The bell holds the time.
Dormition. The falling asleep of Mary, the Orthodox name for the end of her earthly life. Catholics keep the feast as the Assumption.
Your line: she fell asleep. Today, thank one woman who carried you, in a message, a call, or a quiet word if she's gone. Day one thousand forty-eight.
